title: Unbounded evaluation on finitely many clopen geometric sections
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $\Omega$ be an algebraically closed field, and put $P=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $r:V\to P$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme]. Let $I$ be a finite set and let $s_i:P\hookrightarrow V$ for $i\in I$ be pairwise disjoint open immersions with closed images [def-weil-open-immersion, def-weil-closed-immersion], satisfying $rs_i=1_P$. Write $U=\coprod_{i\in I}P$, $j:U\hookrightarrow V$ for their union, and $u=rj:U\to P$ [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-coproduct-family]. Use constant-$A$ module sheaves on the small etale sites and the ordinary unbounded derived categories [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories]. For $K\in D(U_{\mathrm{et}},A)$, write $K_i=s_i^*Dj_!K$ for its restriction to the $i$-th component, using exact inverse image and degreewise extension by zero [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image, def-weil-pbc-extension-by-zero, lem-weil-pbc-extension-by-zero-exact]. The canonical restriction map gives a natural isomorphism
$$Rr_*Dj_!K\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_{i\in I}K_i$$
in $D(P_{\mathrm{et}},A)$, where the derived direct image is computed by K-injective resolutions [def-kun-unbounded-exchange, def-weil-pbc-kinjective-resolutions]. On the clopen decomposition $V=j(U)\amalg(V\setminus j(U))$, a complex is K-injective exactly when its component complexes are K-injective. Thus the displayed isomorphism is normalized by resolutions taken on the $P$ components with zero complex on the complement, followed by the exact global-sections equivalence $\operatorname{Mod}(P_{\mathrm{et}},A)\simeq\operatorname{Mod}_A$ [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-pullback-stalk].
Put $B=Du_{\Sigma!}K=\bigoplus_{i\in I}K_i$ using exact etale sum extension [def-weil-pbc-etale-sum-extension, lem-weil-pbc-etale-restriction-injectives]. Define $\delta_K:r^*B\to Dj_!K$ by the projection $\bigoplus_iK_i\to K_i$ on the component $s_i(P)$ and by zero on the complement. Under $r^*\dashv Rr_*$ [def-kun-unbounded-exchange], its adjunct $a_K:B\to Rr_*Dj_!K$ becomes the canonical finite sum-to-product map. In particular $a_K$ is an isomorphism; after the canonical finite biproduct identification it is the identity, including $I=\varnothing$.

proof.text:
Put $Z=V\setminus j(U)$. Finiteness makes $j(U)$ closed as well as open, so $Z$ is open and closed. The disjoint open cover by $s_i(P)$ and $Z$ identifies $V$ with $\coprod_iP\amalg Z$: maps defined on its pieces glue uniquely, since all overlaps are empty. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-etale-sheaf-clopen-product] to this finite coproduct. Its abelian-sheaf equivalence lifts to constant-$A$ module sheaves: an $A$-action is a family of endomorphisms satisfying the ring identities, and both endomorphisms and their identities are recovered componentwise. Thus restriction is an additive equivalence
$$\mathcal M_V\simeq\bigl(\prod_{i\in I}\mathcal M_P\bigr)\times\mathcal M_Z,\qquad \mathcal M_T=\operatorname{Mod}(T_{\mathrm{et}},A).$$
Kernels and cokernels are determined by their universal properties; the equivalence therefore computes both componentwise and is exact. Applied degreewise it computes cycles, boundaries and cohomology componentwise. In particular acyclicity and quasi-isomorphisms are detected on these pieces. This includes $Z=\varnothing$ and $I=\varnothing$.

source.place: Tag 0A5B, lemma-constant-smooth-statements, first paragraph of proof: finite disjoint-union reduction; explicit module-action and complex extension

proof.text:
Under Step 1, inverse image along $j$ is projection to the $P$ components, and inverse image along $u$ is the diagonal family, since $rs_i=1_P$. Here [lem-weil-pbc-etale-inverse-image-restriction] identifies etale inverse image with actual restriction, including its unit; its formulas also respect $A$-linear maps and actions. By [lem-weil-pbc-extension-by-zero-adjunction], $j_!$ is left adjoint to the projection. The tuple $(F_i,0)$ is its left adjoint too, since
$$\operatorname{Hom}((F_i,0),(G_i,G_Z))=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(F_i,G_i).$$
The unique comparison of these left adjoints identifies $j_!F$ with $(F_i,0)$, with identity restriction on each component. Exactness [lem-weil-pbc-extension-by-zero-exact] gives the same description of $Dj_!$ on complexes and after localization. For a complex $C$ representing $K$, write $C_i$ for its component; then $QC_i=K_i$.

source.place: Tags 03S2/03S3 (section-extension-by-zero, definition-extension-zero) and 03S4 (exercise-jshriek-direct); clopen left-adjoint calculation

proof.text:
For complexes $E,J$ on $V$, Step 1 identifies the Hom complex of [def-weil-pbc-kinjective-resolutions] with
$$\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(E,J)=\Bigl(\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(E_i,J_i)\Bigr)\times\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(E_Z,J_Z).$$
Indeed interchange the degree-indexed product with the finite component product; the differential $d_Jf-(-1)^nf d_E$ is componentwise. A finite product of complexes of abelian groups has cycles and boundaries equal to the products of the corresponding cycles and boundaries (choose a preimage in each of the finitely many coordinates), hence is acyclic when all factors are. If each $J_i,J_Z$ is K-injective this formula proves that $J$ is K-injective. Conversely, test against acyclic $E$ supported on just one component, with zero complexes on the others; the Hom complex then equals that component's Hom complex. This proves the claimed equivalence, including for the two-piece decomposition $j(U)\amalg Z$. The zero complex is K-injective because every such Hom complex is zero.

source.place: Definition 070H (definition-K-injective), expanded using the finite clopen Hom-complex formula

proof.text:
Choose resolutions $\rho_i:C_i\to J_i$ by [prop-weil-pbc-kinjective-resolutions-exist]. Reassemble $(J_i,0)$ on $V$ and call it $J$. Steps 1–3 give a quasi-isomorphism $q:j_!C\to J$ with $J$ K-injective. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-total-derived] computes $Rr_*Dj_!K$ by $Q(r_*J)$. For every etale $W\to P$, [def-weil-pbc-direct-image] gives $(r_*J)(W)=J(W\times_PV)$. The decomposition in Step 1 pulls back to this object; on its $i$-th piece $W\times_PP=W$, and its complement contributes zero. The sheaf axiom on this disjoint cover therefore gives, degreewise and with its actual restriction maps,
$$r_*J\xrightarrow{\sim}\prod_iJ_i.$$
The comparison is precisely restriction to the $s_i$ components. Finite products of complexes in $\mathcal M_P$ preserve quasi-isomorphisms: by the exact equivalence [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-pullback-stalk] this reduces to the finite product cycle/boundary calculation of Step 3 for $A$-modules. Consequently $\prod_i\rho_i$ identifies $Q(\prod_iJ_i)$ with $\prod_iK_i$, proving the displayed isomorphism with the required zero complement normalization. No assumption on the cohomological dimension or properness of $r$ was used.

proof.text: These identifications are natural in the unbounded derived category. By [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-hom-derived], a morphism between the chosen K-injective resolutions is represented by a unique homotopy class of chain maps; a change of resolution is a homotopy equivalence. Restriction and $r_*$ are additive, so preserve chain homotopies. The sectionwise restriction isomorphism of Step 4 commutes with every chain map, hence with its homotopy class and every derived morphism. This also proves independence of resolution choices. The exact global-sections equivalence of [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-point-pullback-stalk] can be applied to the complexes on $P$. By [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-derived-functor], its unbounded derived functor is its degreewise functor with the canonical comparison. Thus the final passage to $A$-module complexes introduces no further resolution or normalization choice.

source.place: Tag 070I (lemma-K-injective), equivalence of homotopy and derived morphisms into K-injectives; Tag 015F (lemma-right-derived-exact-functor)

proof.text: Use [lem-weil-pbc-etale-restriction-injectives] for $u$: its sum extension is exact and left adjoint to inverse image. On the product decomposition of $U$, inverse image from $P$ is the diagonal functor. Its left adjoint is $(F_i)\mapsto\bigoplus_iF_i$, since maps out of that sum are exactly the families $F_i\to M$. The comparison preserves the adjunction bijection and its injections, so degreewise sum extension represents $B$ by $D_C=\bigoplus_iC_i$. Under Steps 1–2, $r^*D_C$ has component $D_C$ on every $s_i(P)$. The prescribed map $\delta_K$ is represented by the chain map $r^*D_C\to j_!C$ with components $\pi_i:D_C\to C_i$ and zero on $Z$. Its composite with $q$ has components $\rho_i\pi_i$ and zero on $Z$.

source.place: Tags 03S3 (definition-extension-zero), 03S5 (proposition-describe-jshriek): exact etale sum extension and its adjunction; finite diagonal/sum adjunction

proof.text:
By [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact], the sheaf adjunction $r^*\dashv r_*$ has exact left adjoint. Its canonical derived adjunction is supplied by [lem-pc-derived-adjoint-functors]. It is computed here by the degreewise adjunction: $J$ is K-injective, and $r_*J$ is K-injective because
$$\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(E,r_*J)=\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(r^*E,J)$$
and exact $r^*$ carries acyclic $E$ to acyclic complexes. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-hom-derived] on both sides. Under the sheaf adjunction, the map of Step 6 sends a local section $b$ of $D_C$ to the family $(\rho_i\pi_i(b))_i$ of sections of $r_*J$: on $s_i(P)$ the pullback is along $rs_i=1_P$, so its adjunction is the identity adjunction; the complement contributes zero. Thus the adjunct is the localization of
$$D_C\xrightarrow{(\rho_i\pi_i)_i}\prod_iJ_i.$$
After the inverse comparison $Q(\prod_i\rho_i)$ from Step 4, its $i$-th projection is $\pi_i$. It is therefore the canonical finite sum-to-product map. Its inverse is $ (x_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i\iota_i(x_i)$: the component equations $\pi_i\iota_k=0$ for $i\ne k$ and $\pi_i\iota_i=1$ verify both inverse identities. These equations hold for complexes and survive localization. After the canonical biproduct identification the adjunct is consequently the identity. For $I=\varnothing$, both complexes and both maps are zero, and the unique endomorphism of zero is its identity.
